claim: Prokaryotes acquire genes from the environment via lateral gene transfer (LGT).
source: Prokaryotes acquire genes from the environment via lateral gene transfer (LGT).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about prokaryotic gene acquisition mechanisms.

claim: Recombination of environmental DNA can prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations.
source: Recombination of environmental DNA can prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations, but LGT was abandoned by the first eukaryotes in favour of sexual reproduction.
evidence: This draws from established understanding of recombination benefits in evolutionary biology.

claim: LGT was abandoned by the first eukaryotes in favour of sexual reproduction.
source: Recombination of environmental DNA can prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations, but LGT was abandoned by the first eukaryotes in favour of sexual reproduction.
evidence: This is a central premise of the paper based on evolutionary understanding.

claim: The greater complexity of eukaryotes is linked with larger genomes.
source: The greater complexity of eukaryotes is linked with larger genomes and we demonstrate that the benefit of LGT declines rapidly with genome size.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic genome characteristics.

claim: The benefit of LGT declines rapidly with genome size.
source: The greater complexity of eukaryotes is linked with larger genomes and we demonstrate that the benefit of LGT declines rapidly with genome size.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The degeneration of larger genomes can only be resisted by increases in recombination length to the same order as genome size.
source: The degeneration of larger genomes can only be resisted by increases in recombination length, to the same order as genome size – as occurs in meiosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model simulations shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Increases in recombination length to the same order as genome size occurs in meiosis.
source: The degeneration of larger genomes can only be resisted by increases in recombination length, to the same order as genome size – as occurs in meiosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiotic recombination.

claim: Sexual reproduction breaks up advantageous combinations of alleles.
source: Sexual reproduction breaks up advantageous combinations of alleles, halves the number of genes transmitted to the offspring, and is less efficient and energetically more costly than asexual reproduction (Bell, 1982; Otto and Lenormand, 2002; Otto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on the costs of sex.

claim: Sexual reproduction halves the number of genes transmitted to the offspring.
source: Sexual reproduction breaks up advantageous combinations of alleles, halves the number of genes transmitted to the offspring, and is less efficient and energetically more costly than asexual reproduction (Bell, 1982; Otto and Lenormand, 2002; Otto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on the costs of sex.

claim: Sexual reproduction is less efficient and energetically more costly than asexual reproduction.
source: Sexual reproduction breaks up advantageous combinations of alleles, halves the number of genes transmitted to the offspring, and is less efficient and energetically more costly than asexual reproduction (Bell, 1982; Otto and Lenormand, 2002; Otto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on the costs of sex.

claim: Sex is a universal feature of eukaryotic life.
source: In spite of these disadvantages sex is a universal feature of eukaryotic life.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic biology.

claim: The presence of common molecular machinery widespread among all eukaryotic lineages is a strong indication that the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA) was already a fully sexual organism.
source: The presence of common molecular machinery, widespread among all eukaryotic lineages, is a strong indication that the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA) was already a fully sexual organism (Schurko and Logsdon, 2008; Speijer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on LECA and meiotic machinery.

claim: Meiotic genes are commonly found in putative asexual eukaryotes, including Amoebozoa.
source: Meiotic genes are commonly found in putative asexual eukaryotes, including Amoebozoa (Lahr et al., 2011; Hofstatter et al., 2018), Diplomonads (Ramesh et al., 2005), Choanoflagellates (Carr et al., 2010) and even lineages once thought to be early diverging such as Trichonomas vaginalis (Malik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies finding meiotic genes in these organisms.

claim: Meiotic genes are commonly found in putative asexual eukaryotes, including Diplomonads.
source: Meiotic genes are commonly found in putative asexual eukaryotes, including Amoebozoa (Lahr et al., 2011; Hofstatter et al., 2018), Diplomonads (Ramesh et al., 2005), Choanoflagellates (Carr et al., 2010) and even lineages once thought to be early diverging such as Trichonomas vaginalis (Malik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies finding meiotic genes in these organisms.

claim: Meiotic genes are commonly found in putative asexual eukaryotes, including Choanoflagellates.
source: Meiotic genes are commonly found in putative asexual eukaryotes, including Amoebozoa (Lahr et al., 2011; Hofstatter et al., 2018), Diplomonads (Ramesh et al., 2005), Choanoflagellates (Carr et al., 2010) and even lineages once thought to be early diverging such as Trichonomas vaginalis (Malik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies finding meiotic genes in these organisms.

claim: Meiotic genes are commonly found in Trichonomas vaginalis.
source: Meiotic genes are commonly found in putative asexual eukaryotes, including Amoebozoa (Lahr et al., 2011; Hofstatter et al., 2018), Diplomonads (Ramesh et al., 2005), Choanoflagellates (Carr et al., 2010) and even lineages once thought to be early diverging such as Trichonomas vaginalis (Malik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies finding meiotic genes in these organisms.

claim: Eukaryotic asexuality is not ancestral but a secondarily evolved state.
source: Eukaryotic asexuality is not ancestral but a secondarily evolved state.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of meiotic genes in putatively asexual lineages.

claim: Phylogenomic analysis shows that eukaryotes arose from the endosymbiosis between an archaeal host and a bacterial endosymbiont, the ancestor of mitochondria.
source: Phylogenomic analysis shows that eukaryotes arose from the endosymbiosis between an archaeal host and a bacterial endosymbiont, the ancestor of mitochondria (Müller et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2015; Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to phylogenomic studies.

claim: The presence of energy-producing endosymbionts allowed the first eukaryotes to escape the bioenergetic constraints that limit the genome size and cellular complexity of prokaryotes.
source: The presence of energy-producing endosymbionts allowed the first eukaryotes to escape the bioenergetic constraints that limit the genome size and cellular complexity of prokaryotes (Lane and Martin, 2010; Lane, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on bioenergetic constraints.

claim: The symbiont genome underwent a massive reduction, with the loss of many redundant gene functions.
source: As with other endosymbioses, the symbiont genome underwent a massive reduction, with the loss of many redundant gene functions (Timmis et al., 2004; López-Madrigal and Gil, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on endosymbiotic genome reduction.

claim: Symbiont release of DNA into the host's cytosol caused the repeated transfer of genes to the host genome, many of which were retained, contributing to the massive genome size expansion during early eukaryotic evolution.
source: Alongside this, symbiont release of DNA into the host's cytosol caused the repeated transfer of genes to the host genome, many of which were retained, contributing to the massive genome size expansion during early eukaryotic evolution (Timmis et al., 2004; Martin and Koonin, 2006; Lane, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on endosymbiotic gene transfer.

claim: Both the host and the endosymbiont, like modern archaea and proteobacteria, are likely to have been capable of transformation.
source: Both the host and the endosymbiont, like modern archaea and proteobacteria, are likely to have been capable of transformation – the uptake of exogenous DNA from the environment followed by homologous recombination (Bernstein and Bernstein, 2013; Vos et al., 2015; Ambur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on transformation in archaea and bacteria.

claim: Transformation involves the acquisition of foreign DNA, the recognition of homologous sequences and recombination, and therefore presents striking similarities with meiosis in eukaryotes.
source: This process involves the acquisition of foreign DNA, the recognition of homologous sequences and recombination, and therefore presents striking similarities with meiosis in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic similarities between the two processes.

claim: The Rad51/Dcm1 gene family, which plays a central role in meiosis, has high protein sequence similarity with RecA, which promotes homologous search and recombination in prokaryotes.
source: The Rad51/Dcm1 gene family, which plays a central role in meiosis, has high protein sequence similarity with RecA, which promotes homologous search and recombination in prokaryotes (Lin et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on protein sequence similarity.

claim: It has been suggested that RecA was acquired by the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes via endosymbiosis from its bacterial endosymbiont.
source: It has been suggested that RecA was acquired by the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes via endosymbiosis from its bacterial endosymbiont (Lin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study proposing this hypothesis.

claim: The Rad51/Dcm1 family could have evolved from archaeal homologs of RadA.
source: Alternatively, the Rad51/Dcm1 family could have evolved from archaeal homologs of RadA (Seitz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study proposing this alternative hypothesis.

claim: The presence of common molecular machinery and the striking similarities between transformation and meiosis suggest that meiosis evolved from bacterial transformation.
source: Regardless, the presence of this common molecular machinery and the striking similarities between these processes suggest that meiosis evolved from bacterial transformation (Schurko and Logsdon, 2008; Bernstein and Bernstein, 2013; Mirzaghaderi and Hörandl, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing this evolutionary relationship.

claim: Recombination can eliminate the linkage between beneficial and deleterious alleles due to Hill-Robertson effects.
source: Recombination can eliminate the linkage between beneficial and deleterious alleles due to Hill-Robertson effects (Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976; Barton and Otto, 2005), increase adaptability in rapidly changing (Hamilton, 1980; Gandon and Otto, 2007; Jokela et al., 2009) or spatially heterogeneous (Pylkov et al., 1998; Lenormand and Otto, 2000) environments, and prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations due to drift predicted by Muller's ratchet for asexual populations (Muller, 1964; Haigh, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies on recombination benefits.

claim: Recombination can increase adaptability in rapidly changing environments.
source: Recombination can eliminate the linkage between beneficial and deleterious alleles due to Hill-Robertson effects (Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976; Barton and Otto, 2005), increase adaptability in rapidly changing (Hamilton, 1980; Gandon and Otto, 2007; Jokela et al., 2009) or spatially heterogeneous (Pylkov et al., 1998; Lenormand and Otto, 2000) environments, and prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations due to drift predicted by Muller's ratchet for asexual populations (Muller, 1964; Haigh, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies.

claim: Recombination can increase adaptability in spatially heterogeneous environments.
source: Recombination can eliminate the linkage between beneficial and deleterious alleles due to Hill-Robertson effects (Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976; Barton and Otto, 2005), increase adaptability in rapidly changing (Hamilton, 1980; Gandon and Otto, 2007; Jokela et al., 2009) or spatially heterogeneous (Pylkov et al., 1998; Lenormand and Otto, 2000) environments, and prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations due to drift predicted by Muller's ratchet for asexual populations (Muller, 1964; Haigh, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Recombination can prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations due to drift predicted by Muller's ratchet for asexual populations.
source: Recombination can eliminate the linkage between beneficial and deleterious alleles due to Hill-Robertson effects (Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976; Barton and Otto, 2005), increase adaptability in rapidly changing (Hamilton, 1980; Gandon and Otto, 2007; Jokela et al., 2009) or spatially heterogeneous (Pylkov et al., 1998; Lenormand and Otto, 2000) environments, and prevent the accumulation of deleterious mutations due to drift predicted by Muller's ratchet for asexual populations (Muller, 1964; Haigh, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies on Muller's ratchet.

claim: Lateral Gene Transfer (LGT) has been recognised as a major force shaping prokaryotic genomes.
source: Lateral Gene Transfer (LGT) has been recognised as a major force shaping prokaryotic genomes (Ochman et al., 2000; Lapierre and Gogarten, 2009; Vos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on LGT in prokaryotes.

claim: Transformation is the only LGT mechanism to be exclusively encoded by genes present on prokaryotic chromosomes.
source: Unlike conjugation and transduction, mediated respectively by plasmids and phages, transformation is the only LGT mechanism to be exclusively encoded by genes present on prokaryotic chromosomes (Ambur et al., 2016), and is maintained by natural selection because it provides benefits analogous to those of sexual recombination (Vos, 2009; Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Wylie et al., 2010; Takeuchi et al., 2014; Vos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on transformation mechanisms.

claim: Transformation is maintained by natural selection because it provides benefits analogous to those of sexual recombination.
source: Unlike conjugation and transduction, mediated respectively by plasmids and phages, transformation is the only LGT mechanism to be exclusively encoded by genes present on prokaryotic chromosomes (Ambur et al., 2016), and is maintained by natural selection because it provides benefits analogous to those of sexual recombination (Vos, 2009; Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Wylie et al., 2010; Takeuchi et al., 2014; Vos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies on transformation benefits.

claim: Recombination via transformation allows adaptation by breaking down disadvantageous combinations of alleles.
source: Recombination via transformation allows adaptation by breaking down disadvantageous combinations of alleles (Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Wylie et al., 2010) and preventing the fixation of deleterious mutations (Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Recombination via transformation prevents the fixation of deleterious mutations.
source: Recombination via transformation allows adaptation by breaking down disadvantageous combinations of alleles (Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Wylie et al., 2010) and preventing the fixation of deleterious mutations (Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Some theoretical studies suggest that transformation is only advantageous in the presence of strong positive epistasis.
source: Some theoretical studies (Redfield, 1988; Redfield et al., 1997) suggest that transformation is only advantageous in the presence of strong positive epistasis, a condition rarely met by extant prokaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Strong positive epistasis is a condition rarely met by extant prokaryotes.
source: Some theoretical studies (Redfield, 1988; Redfield et al., 1997) suggest that transformation is only advantageous in the presence of strong positive epistasis, a condition rarely met by extant prokaryotes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about prokaryotic genetics.

claim: More recent modelling work shows that transformation facilitates the elimination of deleterious mutations and prevents Muller's ratchet.
source: But more recent modelling work shows that transformation facilitates the elimination of deleterious mutations and prevents Muller's ratchet (Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Takeuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent theoretical studies.

claim: Previous models of transformation either do not consider genome size explicitly or treat it as a constant parameter.
source: We know very little about the relation between genome size and the accumulation of deleterious mutations in populations undergoing transformation, as previous models either do not consider it explicitly (Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Wylie et al., 2010) or treat it as a constant parameter (Takeuchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical studies.

claim: Large genomes gain de novo mutations at a faster rate than small ones.
source: Large genomes gain de novo mutations at a faster rate than small ones, leading to a decline in LLC extinction time, as there are more independent loci that can possibly fix for the mutant (Figure 2, no LGT).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: LGT reduces the severity of the ratchet and increases the expected LLC extinction time.
source: LGT reduces the severity of the ratchet and increases the expected LLC extinction time (Figure 2), making the population less vulnerable to stochastic fluctuations in population size.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: As genome size increases, the rate of mutation accumulation markedly increases, both genome wide and per locus.
source: As genome size increases, the rate of mutation accumulation markedly increases, both genome wide and per locus (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Even in presence of LGT, large genomes are subjected to higher rates of accumulation, comparable to those of a purely clonal population.
source: But even in presence of LGT, large genomes are subjected to higher rates of accumulation, comparable to those of a purely clonal population (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutations preferentially accumulate in the accessory genome, where the strength of selection is lower, while the core genome accumulates mutations at a relatively slow rate.
source: Under this selection regime, mutations preferentially accumulate in the accessory genome, where the strength of selection is lower, while the core genome accumulates mutations at a relatively slow rate (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Genome size expansion results in more severe ratchet effects, with a marked increase in the rate of mutations reaching fixation in the regions of the genome that are under weaker selection.
source: Genome size expansion results in more severe ratchet effects, with a marked increase in the rate of mutations reaching fixation in the regions of the genome that are under weaker selection, alongside a moderate increase in core genome mutation fixation rate (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 6.

claim: LGT is effective in reducing the mutational burden, both in the accessory and in the core genome.
source: LGT is effective in reducing the mutational burden, both in the accessory and in the core genome; but this beneficial effect is less evident in large genomes than in small ones (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The beneficial effect of LGT is less evident in large genomes than in small ones.
source: LGT is effective in reducing the mutational burden, both in the accessory and in the core genome; but this beneficial effect is less evident in large genomes than in small ones (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Asexual organisms are vulnerable to the effects of drift, which reduces the genetic variation within a population, causing the progressive and inescapable accumulation of deleterious mutations known as Muller's ratchet.
source: Asexual organisms are well known to be vulnerable to the effects of drift, which reduces the genetic variation within a population, causing the progressive and inescapable accumulation of deleterious mutations known as Muller's ratchet (Muller, 1964; Haigh, 1978; Otto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies on Muller's ratchet.

claim: In eukaryotes, sexual recombination counters the effects of genetic drift and restores genetic variance, increasing the effectiveness of purifying selection and preventing mutational meltdown.
source: In eukaryotes, sexual recombination counters the effects of genetic drift and restores genetic variance, increasing the effectiveness of purifying selection and preventing mutational meltdown (Otto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review on the benefits of sex.

claim: In prokaryotes, sexual fusion does not occur.
source: In prokaryotes, sexual fusion does not occur.
evidence: This is established knowledge about prokaryotic biology.

claim: The exchange of genetic material in prokaryotes occurs through transformation, the lateral gene transfer and recombination of environmental DNA.
source: But the exchange of genetic material does occur through transformation, the lateral gene transfer (LGT) and recombination of environmental DNA (eDNA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about prokaryotic genetic exchange.

claim: Meiotic recombination likely arose from bacterial transformation.
source: Meiotic recombination likely arose from bacterial transformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarities between the two processes discussed earlier in the manuscript.

claim: In small genomes, LGT is effective at preventing Muller's ratchet, with long extinction times and low rates of mutation accumulation.
source: In small genomes, LGT is effective at preventing Muller's ratchet, with long extinction times (Figure 2) and low rates of mutation accumulation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Large genomes limit the efficiency of LGT, increasing the overall input of mutations to the genome.
source: However, our results show that large genomes limit the efficiency of LGT, increasing the overall input of mutations to the genome.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Larger genomes increase the severity of the ratchet leading to shorter extinction times and faster rates of mutation accumulation.
source: Larger genomes increase the severity of the ratchet leading to shorter extinction times and faster rates of mutation accumulation (Figures 2–3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: Other theoretical studies indicate that LGT can increase the rate of adaptive evolution.
source: In particular, a number of other theoretical studies indicate that LGT can increase the rate of adaptive evolution (Iles et al., 2003; Levin and Cornejo, 2009; Wylie et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: It would be reasonable to expect that adaptive benefits of LGT decline as genome size increases.
source: In light of our results, it would be reasonable to expect these adaptive benefits decline as genome size increases.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the current model.

claim: Theoretical results predict that the severity of the ratchet increases exponentially with genome size.
source: Under the assumption of a constant mutation rate per locus, theoretical results predict that the severity of the ratchet (measured as the equilibrium number of individuals in the least-loaded class) increases exponentially with genome size (Haigh, 1978; Appendix 1; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to theoretical work and reference to the appendix.

claim: Large genomes are penalized by the decreased effectiveness of LGT at reducing the mutation load.
source: In addition to this effect – which could potentially be offset by a lower mutation rate per locus – large genomes are penalized by the decreased effectiveness of LGT at reducing the mutation load.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model results.

claim: Even with a constant genome-wide mutation rate, LGT becomes less effective at purging large genomes from deleterious mutations.
source: Even with a constant genome-wide mutation rate, LGT becomes less effective at purging large genomes from deleterious mutations, showing that this effect is not due to a higher mutation rate, but to an intrinsic limitation of LGT (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 4.

claim: In a number of species, LGT has been estimated as being the same magnitude (or higher) as the rate of nucleotide substitution, including Bacillus cereus.
source: In a number of species, LGT has been estimated as being the same magnitude (or higher) as the rate of nucleotide substitution, including Bacillus cereus (Hao and Golding, 2006), Streptococcus (Marri et al., 2006), Corynebacterium (Marri et al., 2007), and Pseudomonas syringae (Nowell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: LGT rates are highly variable among species.
source: Rates are highly variable among species (Croucher et al., 2012; Vos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Competence for transformation can be induced by a range of environmental stressors including DNA damage, high cell density and limited nutrient availability.
source: Competence for transformation can be induced by a range of environmental stressors including DNA damage, high cell density and limited nutrient availability (Bernstein and Bernstein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review on transformation.

claim: LGT rates are constrained by eDNA availability, which depends on the amount of DNA in the environment and the degree of sequence homology.
source: But LGT rates are constrained by eDNA availability, which depends on the amount of DNA in the environment and the degree of sequence homology (Croucher et al., 2012; Vos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on LGT constraints.

claim: The model predicts that higher LGT rates will strengthen purifying selection and favour the elimination of mutants.
source: The model predicts that higher LGT rates will strengthen purifying selection and favour the elimination of mutants.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results.

claim: This result is compatible with the strong correlation observed between the number of horizontally transferred genes and genome size across a range of prokaryotes.
source: This result is compatible with the strong correlation observed between the number of horizontally transferred genes and genome size across a range of prokaryotes (Jain et al., 2003; Fuchsman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies showing this correlation.

claim: In gram-positive bacteria, recombination of large eDNA sequences is the exception rather than the rule.
source: In gram-positive bacteria, recombination of large eDNA sequences is the exception rather than the rule (Croucher et al., 2012; Mell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Experimental work indicates that the distribution of eDNA length acquired is skewed towards short fragments, with a third of transformation events less than 1kb, a median around 2-6kb and range extending up to ~50kb.
source: Experimental work indicates that the distribution of eDNA length acquired is skewed towards short fragments, with a third of transformation events less than 1kb, a median around 2-6kb and range extending up to ~50kb (Croucher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claim: In Streptococcus pneumoniae, the dedicated system cleaves eDNA into smaller fragments before recombination takes place.
source: This appears to be an evolved state in Streptococcus pneumoniae, as the dedicated system cleaves eDNA into smaller fragments before recombination takes place (Claverys et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claim: Cleavage of eDNA into smaller sequences increases the likelihood of homologous recombination.
source: Cleavage of eDNA into smaller sequences increases the likelihood of homologous recombination, while the acquisition of long sequences can be associated with loss of genetic information (Croucher et al., 2012) and can potentially disrupt regulatory and physiological networks (Bernstein and Bernstein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on recombination mechanisms.

claim: The acquisition of long sequences can be associated with loss of genetic information.
source: Cleavage of eDNA into smaller sequences increases the likelihood of homologous recombination, while the acquisition of long sequences can be associated with loss of genetic information (Croucher et al., 2012) and can potentially disrupt regulatory and physiological networks (Bernstein and Bernstein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on recombination mechanisms.

claim: The acquisition of long sequences can potentially disrupt regulatory and physiological networks.
source: Cleavage of eDNA into smaller sequences increases the likelihood of homologous recombination, while the acquisition of long sequences can be associated with loss of genetic information (Croucher et al., 2012) and can potentially disrupt regulatory and physiological networks (Bernstein and Bernstein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on recombination mechanisms.

claim: It has been suggested that the small size of recombination fragments is a mechanism for preventing the spread of mobile genetic elements.
source: It has also been suggested that the small size of recombination fragments is a mechanism for preventing the spread of mobile genetic elements (Croucher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study proposing this hypothesis.

claim: Gram-negative bacteria do not cleave eDNA on import.
source: On the other hand, gram-negative bacteria do not cleave eDNA on import, but their ability to acquire eDNA sequences >50kb is limited by physical constraints (Mell and Redfield, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claim: The ability of gram-negative bacteria to acquire eDNA sequences >50kb is limited by physical constraints.
source: On the other hand, gram-negative bacteria do not cleave eDNA on import, but their ability to acquire eDNA sequences >50kb is limited by physical constraints (Mell and Redfield, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claim: There is no evidence that larger genome size is accompanied by a higher recombination length.
source: But there is no evidence that larger genome size is accompanied by a higher recombination length.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the lack of empirical evidence.

claim: Bacteria do not load large pieces of chromosome via LGT (i.e. >10% of a genome).
source: To our knowledge bacteria do not load large pieces of chromosome via LGT (i.e. >10% of a genome), although in principle it should be possible for them to do so.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about bacterial LGT practices.

claim: The strength of selection plays a critical role in determining the rate of mutation accumulation.
source: As for purely asexual populations (Haigh, 1978), the strength of selection plays a critical role in determining the rate of mutation accumulation, with regions of the genome under strong selection accumulating mutations at a low rate (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and demonstrated by model results in Figures 5-6.

claim: The ratchet effect is mainly observed in the accessory genome, with mutations accumulating preferentially in loci under weak selection.
source: The ratchet effect is mainly observed in the accessory genome, with mutations accumulating preferentially in loci under weak selection (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figures 5-6.

claim: The model predicts that genome size expansion can occur in populations under strong purifying selection.
source: Our model predicts that genome size expansion can occur in populations under strong purifying selection (e.g. due to a larger effective population size).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results.

claim: Strong selection decreases the rate of genetic information loss, allowing the acquisition of new genetic content without an attendant increase in mutation fixation.
source: Strong selection decreases the rate of genetic information loss, allowing the acquisition of new genetic content without an attendant increase in mutation fixation.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: This prediction is in agreement with the positive correlation observed between genome size and dN/dS in bacteria.
source: This prediction is in agreement with the positive correlation observed between genome size and dN/dS in bacteria (Novichkov et al., 2009; Bobay and Ochman, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Organisms under similar selective pressures often display a broad range of genome sizes.
source: However, organisms under similar selective pressures often display a broad range of genome sizes (Novichkov et al., 2009), indicating that other factors, including mutation rate and LGT, have a strong impact on prokaryotic genome size.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claim: Other factors, including mutation rate and LGT, have a strong impact on prokaryotic genome size.
source: However, organisms under similar selective pressures often display a broad range of genome sizes (Novichkov et al., 2009), indicating that other factors, including mutation rate and LGT, have a strong impact on prokaryotic genome size.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of genome size variation.

claim: Under high mutation rate and weak selective pressure, genome size expansion is disfavoured.
source: Under high mutation rate and weak selective pressure, genome size expansion is disfavoured.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: Eukaryotes, including many protists, typically possess much larger genomes than prokaryotes.
source: Eukaryotes, including many protists, typically possess much larger genomes than prokaryotes (Koonin, 2009; Elliott and Gregory, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on genome size.

claim: Eukaryotic genome size expansion was favoured by the acquisition of an endosymbiont, which evolved into the mitochondrion.
source: Eukaryotic genome size expansion was favoured by the acquisition of an endosymbiont, which evolved into the mitochondrion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic evolution.

claim: The acquisition of mitochondria released bioenergetic constraints on cell size and allowed the evolution of genetic and morphological complexity.
source: This released bioenergetic constraints on cell size and allowed the evolution of genetic and morphological complexity (Lane and Martin, 2010; Lane, 2014; Lane, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on bioenergetic constraints.

claim: The endosymbionts underwent gene loss, a frequently observed process in extant endosymbiotic relationships.
